cues.text: One rung at a time, from the bottom. Everything Part One has built.
Investment means spending a large sum now for revenue later.
Some of that money can never be got back. That is a sunk cost.
The future is uncertain, and you learn about it a little at a time.
The chance to build usually keeps — you can decide next year instead.
So waiting has value: it cuts off the bad half and keeps the good half.
None of that is about disliking risk.
Waiting costs you the profit you give up, so there is a level high enough to act.
That level — the trigger — sits above the textbook's line.
How far above depends on how choppy revenue is and what money costs.
In the base case, nearly double. In a rough trade, over three times.
Cheaper money raises the trigger, because information is worth more.
The same logic in reverse means she absorbs real losses before quitting.
So the band where doing nothing is right is about nine times wider than the textbook's.
Walk revenue up through the band and back down, and the effect stays behind.
That is hysteresis, and it explains the dollar and the imports.
Cushion a firm's downside and it invests early; protect its upside and it stays.
Put many such firms together and the whole industry looks frozen — correctly.
And the master scale in its final form. Give up at nought point seven two. Build at one point six two. And in between, a wide stretch where the right thing to do is nothing.
It does not say firms are irrational. It says the opposite.
It does not say waiting is always right.
And it does not apply where a rival can snatch the opportunity away from you.
So go back to the two people we opened with, and let Nell explain them.
The farmer keeps going because closing is final. Staying open keeps the good years possible, and that is worth more to him than the losses are costing him.
And I do not build, because building is final too. Waiting another year is worth something, and this year's numbers are not yet good enough to pay for it.
One more thing before we stop. A government somewhere spent hundreds of billions of pounds on a policy that assumed none of this was true.
Everything in Part One, in one ladder.
The paper does not say firms are irrational, or that waiting is always right.
Part Two uses all of it on a policy that cost hundreds of billions.
